label: Prehistoric Japan
pitch:
Fourteen thousand years before Buddhism arrived and pulled Japan into recorded history, someone on the archipelago made a pot — and started one of the longest, strangest, most independent cultural runs anywhere on Earth. The Jomon were hunter-gatherers who fired clay vessels millennia before farming, built 500-person settlements without grain, and carved goggle-eyed clay figurines that still look like aliens. Then around 900 BCE rice and metal arrived together from Korea, and within a few centuries the islands had been transformed into a land of moated rice-farming villages, bronze ritual bells, and a hundred warring chiefdoms. By 250 CE, somebody invented the keyhole-shaped tomb, and the Yamato clan started building the largest tumuli in the world. The endpoint is 538 CE, when Baekje envoys carried a Buddha statue and a bag of sutras into the Yamato court — and the prehistoric era ended in one diplomatic gift.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Jomon Pottery from ~14,000 BCE is among the oldest fired ceramics on Earth, predating Near Eastern pottery by thousands of years
• The Sannai-Maruyama Settlement housed up to 500 people for sixteen hundred years on chestnuts and fish, with no agriculture
• The Gold Seal of the King of Na, dug up by a farmer in 1784, is physical proof of Chinese-Japanese diplomacy in 57 CE
• Queen Himiko of Yamatai is the first Japanese person whose existence is confirmed by a written source — written by Chinese chroniclers, not Japanese ones
• The Daisen Kofun is the largest tomb in the world by surface area — built by a polity that had no writing

🤔 Why It Matters: Japan's prehistoric era is the world's clearest counter-example to the standard story that civilization requires farming. The Jomon ran complex coastal society for 13,000 years on nuts and fish; the Yayoi imported the entire Bronze Age + Iron Age package as a single bundle from Korea; the Kofun built monuments that rival the pyramids without ever writing a sentence. Everything that came afterward — the emperor, the samurai, modern Japan — grew from roots planted in the millennia covered here.

🎲 Wild Card: The Jomon shakoki-dogu figurines, with their huge goggle-like eyes, look uncannily like a person wearing a snow goggles or a space helmet — a resemblance that has fueled decades of pseudoarchaeological alien-contact theories. They are almost certainly not aliens. They are almost certainly fertility figures or healing effigies, ritually broken to absorb illness or misfortune.

spans.label: Jomon Pottery Era
spans.description: One of the longest continuous cultural traditions in human history. Hunter-gatherers on the Japanese archipelago made the world's oldest pottery, lived in pit-house villages, traded jade and obsidian across hundreds of miles of open ocean, and built 500-person settlements like Sannai-Maruyama — all without farming.

spans.label: Yayoi Rice Revolution
spans.description: Wet-rice agriculture, bronze, and iron arrived together from the Korean peninsula, brought by migrants who crossed the Korea Strait. Moated villages replaced pit-house hamlets, social stratification appeared, and a hundred warring chiefdoms competed for the best paddy land. Chinese chronicles document the first named Japanese rulers.

spans.label: Yamato Confederation Forming
spans.description: The hundred warring kingdoms of Yayoi Japan began coalescing into larger confederations, briefly under the shaman queen Himiko of Yamatai (whose location is still debated). Out of this consolidation emerged the Yamato clan, ancestor of the imperial line that exists today.

spans.label: Kofun Tomb Period
spans.description: Enormous keyhole-shaped tombs began rising from the plains of central Japan, including the Daisen Kofun — the largest tomb in the world by area. The Yamato court consolidated political dominance across Honshu and northern Kyushu through marriage alliances, ritual authority, and the threat of force, while waves of Korean immigrants brought iron, sueki stoneware, and writing.

spans.label: Pre-Buddhist Threshold
spans.description: The final decades before recorded history. Korean ceramic and metal technology peaked, the Soga clan rose at court, and in 538 (or 552, depending on the source) the Baekje king sent a Buddha statue and Buddhist sutras to the Yamato court — ending the prehistoric era and triggering the religious-political crisis that would define the next century.

events.label: Odai Yamamoto Pottery
events.description: Clay potsherds from the Odai Yamamoto site in Aomori, northern Honshu, radiocarbon-dated to around 14,500 BCE, are among the oldest pottery on Earth, made by hunter-gatherers long before farming, cities, or writing existed anywhere.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A 1998 dig recovered just 46 small fragments, and most of them came from a single vessel. The dating leaned on charred food residue still stuck to the sherds, which gave radiocarbon ages of roughly 11,800 to 11,500 BCE that, once calibrated, push back to about 14,500 BCE (around 16,500 years before present). Pottery of a similar great age has surfaced only in a few spots on the Asian mainland, such as sites on the lower Amur River, making this one of humanity's earliest experiments with fired clay.

events.label: Incipient Jomon Pottery
events.description: The opening phase of the Jomon period, when scattered groups across the islands took up pot-making over roughly two thousand years. These earliest vessels were plain, deep, often pointed-bottomed cooking pots; the famous cord-marking came much later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Archaeologists slice the roughly 14,000-year Jomon era into six phases, and this opening stretch — the Incipient Jomon — runs the longest, somewhere between 13,000 and 8,000 BCE depending on whose chronology you use. The pots had pointed or rounded bottoms rather than flat ones, which sounds impractical until you remember they were meant to be wedged into the embers and ash of a fire, not stood on a table. One early site at Shinonouchi in Nagano has yielded simple vessels dated to around 13,000 BCE. Cord-marking — rolling a twisted plant-fiber cord across the wet clay — only became widespread later, which is why the very oldest Jomon pots are smooth and undecorated.

events.label: End of the Last Ice Age
events.description: The boundary, around 11,700 BCE, where geologists end the Pleistocene ice age and begin the warm Holocene we still live in. As the ice melted and seas rose, the land bridges to the Asian mainland drowned and Japan became a true island chain.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The cold snap just before this boundary — the Younger Dryas, a roughly 1,200-year relapse into glacial conditions from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago — was likely triggered by floods of meltwater pouring off the collapsing North American ice sheets and disrupting ocean currents. At the peak of the Ice Age, seas sat about 400 feet (120 m) lower than today, enough to expose dry-land connections across the shallow straits. The water did not stop rising at the Holocene boundary, though: it kept climbing for another six thousand years, and in central and eastern Japan it actually overshot, peaking about 10 feet (3 m) higher than the modern shoreline around 6,000 years ago — a drowning of the coast that geologists call the Jomon transgression.

events.label: Jomon Pit Dwellings
events.description: The standard Jomon home: a semi-sunken pit house (tateana-jukyo) with a floor dug a few feet into the ground, a frame of wooden posts, a thatched or bark roof, and a central hearth. The buried floor traded the cold and the typhoons for an insulated, low-slung shelter that kept a family of five or six snug.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The design was so good it barely changed for ten thousand years and was still being built in rural Japan into the historical period. Roofs usually rested on four posts, though builders used anywhere from two to five or more, and in cold northern areas the pit could be sunk a full yard (about a meter) deep to trap ground warmth. Most houses lasted only a decade or two before the buried timbers rotted, so a household simply dug a fresh pit nearby and moved over, which is why Jomon village sites are riddled with overlapping old floors.

events.label: Earliest Lacquerware
events.description: Jomon craftspeople refined the toxic sap of the urushi tree into lacquer, coating combs, bowls, and ornaments in durable, glossy finishes, often colored red. It launched a tradition that has run unbroken in Japan for some nine thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The current record-holder is a roughly 9,000-year-old red-lacquered object from the Kakinoshima B site in Hakodate, Hokkaido, believed to be the oldest lacquerware in the world. The lacquer tree itself goes back even further: a specimen carbon-dated at the Torihama shell mound came in around 12,600 years old, the oldest urushi tree yet found. Turning raw sap into a usable coating takes months of refining, and the prized red came from grinding in either iron oxide or cinnabar (a mercury mineral), a genuinely sophisticated chemistry for the Stone Age.

events.label: Jomon Shell Middens
events.description: Enormous mounds of discarded shells, fish bones, and tools that piled up over thousands of years along Japan's coasts — the trash heaps of communities that lived off the sea. One near Tokyo became the site of the first scientific excavation ever conducted in Japan.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: More than 2,000 shell middens are scattered across Japan; the largest, the Kasori mounds in Chiba Prefecture, rank among the biggest in the world, with the heaps really building up about 5,000 years ago. The Tokyo discovery was pure luck: the American zoologist Edward Sylvester Morse, who had come to study brachiopods (a kind of shelled marine animal), spotted the Omori mound from the window of a moving train days after arriving in 1877, then dug it that autumn. Far from useless garbage, these mounds are archaeological gold — the calcium from the shells neutralizes the acidic Japanese soil that would otherwise dissolve bone, preserving fish, animal, and even human skeletons that tell us exactly what the Jomon ate and who they were.

events.label: Jomon Dog Domestication
events.description: Dogs were the only animal the Jomon domesticated, and they buried them with evident care, often laid out whole and close to human graves. These were working hunting partners, not livestock.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The oldest known dog burials in Japan come from the Kamikuroiwa rock shelter in Ehime Prefecture, where two dogs were found dated to about 7,400 to 7,200 years ago. The bones, dug up back in 1962, were misplaced for decades and only rediscovered in 2011 in a forgotten corner of a Keio University storeroom. The two animals were small-to-medium dogs that already resembled the later "Jomon dog" type, ancestors of breeds like today's Shiba and Akita.

events.label: Jomon Obsidian Trade Networks
events.description: Jomon communities moved obsidian (volcanic glass, prized for flaking into razor-sharp blades) across long distances, including open water, with stone from the offshore Izu Islands turning up at sites hundreds of miles away. It is hard evidence of organized maritime exchange well beyond a simple forager band.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The key source was Kozushima, a tiny island in the Izu chain that even at the lowest Ice Age sea levels sat across at least 25 miles (40 km) of open ocean, so every piece had to come by boat. The seafaring habit was ancient: Kozushima obsidian shows up at sites on the mainland Kanto Plain dating back around 30,000 years, long before the Jomon themselves. Chemical fingerprinting lets archaeologists match a given flake to its exact volcano, and Kozushima and the inland Wada Pass stone both traveled more than 120 miles (200 km) from where they were quarried.

events.label: Jomon Jade Working
events.description: Around the Itoigawa coast on the Sea of Japan, Jomon craftspeople ground hard green jadeite into polished beads and pendants — quite possibly the oldest worked jade anywhere on Earth, generations before China's celebrated jade cultures got going.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The richest evidence comes from the Chojagahara site near Itoigawa (Niigata Prefecture), an actual jade workshop where finished and half-finished pendants turned up together. X-ray analysis of jade found hundreds of miles away at Sannai-Maruyama and in southern Hokkaido traces the stone back to Itoigawa, proof the Jomon ran long-distance trade networks. The favored shape was the magatama, a curved comma-like bead — a form so enduring it stayed in use through the later Yayoi era and survives in Japanese culture as one of the Three Sacred Treasures of the imperial regalia.

events.label: Sannai-Maruyama Settlement
events.description: Japan's biggest Jomon settlement, on the coast of what is now Aomori Prefecture in northern Honshu. For roughly sixteen centuries it was effectively a town, home to as many as 500 people, with zoned areas for houses, storage, burials, garbage, and ceremony, plus long-distance trade in obsidian and jade.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The famous reconstruction towering over the site is a six-pillar building whose chestnut posts were a yard (about a meter) across, set in holes spaced a precise 14 feet (4.2 meters) apart, hinting that the builders used real surveying. The original post bases were deliberately scorched to fight rot in the damp soil, a trick that also helped preserve them for excavators to find. The site was rediscovered in 1992 when crews were clearing ground for a baseball stadium; the dig was so important the stadium plan was scrapped, and in 2021 Sannai-Maruyama became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

events.label: Chestnut Grove Management
events.description: The people of Sannai-Maruyama tended chestnut groves for food and timber, a kind of tree-farming (arboriculture) that smudges the tidy line between gathering wild food and farming. Preserved chestnuts from the site show reduced genetic diversity, the fingerprint of deliberate human selection.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The clue first came from pollen: chestnut pollen spikes in the soil layers while the village was occupied, far above what a natural forest would shed, suggesting people were clearing competing trees to favor chestnuts. Even more telling, the nuts themselves grew bigger over the generations, and late-Jomon chestnuts from such sites rival the size of modern cultivated varieties, pointing to thousands of years of unconscious or deliberate breeding. Researchers call this halfway state hansaibai (semi-cultivation): not quite farming, but a long way from simply picking what the forest offered.

events.label: Flame-Style Pottery (Kaen-doki)
events.description: Middle Jomon potters along the Shinano River in the Niigata region made flame-style vessels (kaen-doki), their rims erupting into twisting, flame-like coils and tendrils of clay. The flamboyant, fragile rims would never survive daily cooking, marking these as objects for ritual and display.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The style flourished for only about five centuries, roughly 3,400 to 2,400 BCE, and stayed tightly clustered along the Shinano River valley. The type takes its name from the Umataka site in Nagaoka, and a single spectacular pot unearthed at the Sasayama site in Tokamachi in 1982 became the only piece of Jomon pottery ever designated a National Treasure of Japan. Flame pots have toured abroad, including the British Museum, and have no real parallel anywhere else in the prehistoric world.

events.label: Dogu Figurines
events.description: Small clay figurines (dogu) with deliberately exaggerated features: bulging eyes, swollen limbs, and bellies and breasts that suggest pregnancy. Many turn up snapped at the joints, hinting they were ritually "killed," perhaps to carry off a sick person's illness.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Estimates of how many have been found range from about 15,000 (Japan's National Museum of Japanese History) to roughly 18,000, almost all of them female and concentrated in the northern half of the country. They are overwhelmingly a northern and eastern phenomenon, and their numbers exploded in the later, harder centuries of the Jomon. A handful are revered enough to be National Treasures, among them the Jomon Venus, a rounded clay woman dug from the Tanabatake site in Nagano and dated to roughly 3000 to 2000 BCE.

events.label: Shakoki-Dogu
events.description: The goggle-eyed shakoki-dogu — clay figures whose huge slit eyes look like a person squinting through Inuit snow goggles — emerged in northern Honshu late in the Jomon. The name literally means "light-blocking-device figure," after the snow-goggle resemblance; the space-helmet look later spawned a cottage industry of alien-contact theories that no archaeologist takes seriously.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most famous one was dug up at the Kamegaoka site in Tsugaru (Aomori Prefecture) in 1887, is missing its left leg, lives in the Tokyo National Museum today, and is registered as an Important Cultural Property. Around 3,000 of these specifically goggle-eyed figures have been recorded, almost all from the Tohoku region and southern Hokkaido — a slice of the roughly 18,000 dogu of every type found across Japan. Most turn up broken, and the figures often show exaggerated hips, chest, and thighs, which is part of why some researchers read them as fertility or earth-mother images rather than literal portraits.

events.label: Jomon Stone Circles
events.description: Late Jomon communities in northern Honshu hauled in thousands of river stones and laid them out in rings around central standing-stone clusters, ringed by burial pits — gathering places where scattered communities met to bury their dead and mark the turning of the seasons.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Oyu, in Kazuno (Akita Prefecture), is really two circles a stone's throw apart: Manza at 151 feet (46 meters) across — the largest stone circle in Japan — and Nonakado at 138 feet (42 meters). The Jomon didn't use local rock; they carried the rounded river stones from a riverbed roughly 4 miles (7 kilometers) away. The Komakino circle near Aomori City is even wider overall at about 180 feet (55 meters) of concentric rings. Both sites are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage group, and Oyu has been a protected Special National Historic Site since 1956.

events.label: Late Jomon Cooling and Contraction
events.description: A turn toward colder climate thinned the rich nut forests that had fed Jomon prosperity, and populations fell and settlements shrank across central and eastern Japan, setting up the upheaval to come when continental newcomers arrived a few centuries later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Jomon population is estimated to have peaked somewhere around 200,000 to 260,000 people in the Middle period, then slid back toward 100,000 by the end, with the once-crowded east hit hardest. The cooling lines up with a worldwide climate downturn known as the 4.2-kiloyear event (about 2200 BCE), a drying and chilling that disrupted civilizations from Mesopotamia to Egypt around the same time. Sannai-Maruyama, the great northern town, was abandoned right in this window, and skeletons from the later Jomon show signs of nutritional stress.

events.label: Final Jomon Ritual Intensification
events.description: As cooling climate thinned the forests and shrank settlements, the Jomon poured more of their dwindling energy into ceremony — bigger stone circles, fussier burials, and clay figurines cranked out by the thousand — the classic signature of a culture leaning on ritual when the food gets harder to find.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Jomon period ran roughly 14,500 BCE to 300 BCE — about 14,000 years, one of the longest continuous cultural traditions humans have ever managed. The Late and Final phases (about 2000–300 BCE) line up with the Shang and Zhou dynasties in China and the Mycenaeans in Greece, yet Japan stayed entirely without farming, metal, or writing the whole time. Modern DNA studies show the Jomon never truly vanished: present-day Japanese still carry substantial Jomon ancestry, and Hokkaido's Ainu and the people of the Ryukyu Islands carry the most of all.

events.label: Jomon Genetic Heritage
events.description: DNA pulled from ancient Jomon skeletons shows they descended from a distinct East Asian lineage that split off from mainland ancestors deep in the Ice Age. That genetic signature survives most strongly in the Ainu of Hokkaido and the Ryukyu Islanders.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Whole-genome studies estimate the Jomon ancestors parted ways with the populations that became Han Chinese and Koreans somewhere between roughly 38,000 and 18,000 years ago, then evolved in island isolation. The genetic inheritance is wildly uneven across modern Japan: the Ainu carry on the order of 70% Jomon ancestry, while mainland "Yamato" Japanese carry only about 10%, the rest coming from the later wave of farmers who arrived from the continent. Oddly, the Ainu in the far north and the Ryukyuans in the far south are genetically closer to each other than either is to the mainland population sandwiched between them — both kept a heavy Jomon dose because the later migration reached the archipelago's two ends last.

events.label: Wet-Rice Agriculture Arrives
events.description: Wet-rice paddy farming (rice grown in flooded, irrigated fields) crossed from the Korean Peninsula onto northern Kyushu around 900 BCE and surged after 300 BCE — the single most transformative shift in Japanese history before the 1860s, turning a land of foragers into one of competing rice-farming chiefdoms.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A paddy field, properly managed, yields roughly ten times the calories per acre that even the richest forest does, and on a predictable annual schedule — which is why farming villages outbred and outlasted their Jomon neighbors within a few generations. The whole shift from foraging to farming to warfare to states took over 5,000 years in the Near East and about 3,000 in China, but Japan compressed it into under a thousand, because the Korean immigrants imported the entire working bundle rather than inventing any of it. Everything that followed — the Yamato state, the emperor, Buddhism, the samurai — grew from these first paddies.

events.label: Itazuke Rice Paddies
events.description: The Itazuke site in Fukuoka, on northern Kyushu, holds some of the oldest known rice paddies in Japan — built with dikes and irrigation channels diverting water from a nearby river, using techniques identical to contemporary Korean rice farming. Direct evidence the agricultural package arrived by migration, not local invention.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Itazuke is also Japan's oldest known moated settlement, ringed by a defensive ditch — a sign that the violence and territorial competition of the rice economy showed up almost as early as the rice itself. Some paddy traces here actually date to the very end of the Jomon period, which scrambled the old textbook line that wet-rice farming began only with the Yayoi. The site was also where Yayoi pottery first turned up alongside metal tools: bronze spears and swords came out of a tomb here, the first time the new pottery was found paired with metalwork. Itazuke shares its "oldest rice village" claim with the Nabatake site at Karatsu in nearby Saga.

events.label: Toraijin Migration from Korea
events.description: Continental immigrants from the Korean Peninsula — called toraijin ("people who came across") in later Japanese sources — arrived in waves on northern Kyushu, bringing rice, bronze, and iron. They were physically distinct from the Jomon (taller, narrower-faced), and modern DNA confirms a real population influx, not just borrowed ideas.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A 2021 ancient-DNA study in Science Advances overturned the old two-part picture and found modern Japanese carry a tripartite ancestry: indigenous Jomon, the rice-farming Yayoi immigrants who carried Northeast Asian ancestry, and a third large wave of broadly East Asian ancestry that arrived later in the Kofun period (roughly the 3rd to 7th centuries CE). The Jomon themselves had been a tiny, isolated population — an effective size of around 1,000 — cut off from the mainland for some 15,000 to 20,000 years after rising seas turned Japan into islands. Genetic work on a skeleton from the Doigahama site in Yamaguchi, a Yayoi cemetery holding over 300 individuals, has linked these newcomers closely to mainland Northeast Asian groups.

events.label: Bronze and Iron Introduced
events.description: Bronze and iron reached Japan together through Korean and Chinese sources — unlike the Near East, where bronze led iron by nearly 2,000 years. The Japanese split them by job: bronze for ritual objects (bells, mirrors), iron for the practical cutting work (hoes, axes, sickles, real weapons).

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Getting both metals at once let the Yayoi make a deliberate choice rather than follow a fixed sequence, and the logic was simple physics — bronze is beautiful and easy to cast but soft, while iron is tougher and holds an edge, so iron got the tools and weapons and bronze got the gods. This same "bronze for the gods, iron for the world" split shows up on the Korean Peninsula in the same era, a clue the Japanese were adapting a continental pattern rather than blindly copying it. Iron also rusts away in the ground, so it survives far worse than bronze in the archaeological record, which can make bronze look more common in finds than it actually was in daily life.

events.label: Dotaku Bronze Bells
events.description: Dotaku are bronze bells, some over three feet tall, cast in the Kinai region (around modern Osaka and Nara) and buried on hilltops or in remote spots — most without clappers, apparently never rung. Likely ritual objects tied to the farming cycle, hundreds have been found, none carrying any inscription to explain them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The biggest single bell, 134.7 cm tall (about 4 ft 5 in) and now in the Tokyo National Museum, came from a cache of fourteen accidentally dug up by two teenage boys on a Shiga hillside in 1881. The largest hoard turned up in 1996 when a farm-road bulldozer in Kamo, Shimane, struck a buried cache of 39 bells, many "nested" with a small bell tucked inside a larger one. Early small dotaku do seem to have actually sounded — they have holes for a pendulum clapper — but over the centuries the bells grew taller, more elaborately decorated with scenes of hunting and harvesting, and steadily less functional, drifting from instruments into pure ritual deposits. Nothing comparable exists in Korea, China, or anywhere else.

events.label: Yayoi Pottery Style
events.description: Yayoi pottery — thin-walled, smooth, often reddish-brown, made for cooking and storing rice rather than ritual display — replaced the wild flame pots of the Jomon. You can sort the two into separate piles in five seconds; the aesthetic jump from exuberant art to plain utility mirrors the shift from foraging to farming.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The whole period is named for a Tokyo neighborhood almost by accident: in 1884 a University of Tokyo prep-school student, Shozo Arisaka, dug a single distinctive red-clay jar out of a shell mound at Mukogaoka, in the Yayoi district of Bunkyo ward. The find was reported to scholars in an 1889 journal, the pottery style took its name from the neighborhood, and the entire era was named after the pottery. Awkwardly, archaeologists were never able to pin down the exact mound, so the protected national site is officially called the "Yayoi 2-chome Site" rather than the Mukogaoka Shell Mound.

events.label: Yayoi Warfare
events.description: Yayoi skeletons across Kyushu and western Japan carry the marks of real warfare — arrowheads lodged in bone, sword cuts on skulls, headless bodies — and villages grew defensive, ringed by ditches, palisades, and watchtowers. The Jomon had shown almost no organized violence; the Yayoi world was soaked in it, all of it flowing from rice and the surplus worth fighting over.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: One Doigahama burial held an adult man with fifteen stone arrowheads driven into his bones from chest to waist — apparently shot at point-blank range, probably a defender of his village. A study by Okayama University researchers found this hyper-violence peaked in the Middle Yayoi, roughly 350 BCE to 25 CE. The era's defenses culminate at Yoshinogari in Saga, Japan's largest Yayoi site, ringed by a V-shaped outer moat about 1.6 miles (2.5 km) long enclosing some 100 acres (40 hectares), studded with watchtowers and fences — and its coffins held bodies with arrowheads still embedded and some missing their heads entirely.

events.label: Yoshinogari Settlement
events.description: Yoshinogari in northern Kyushu is the largest known Yayoi settlement: a fortified, moated town bristling with watchtowers and raised storehouses, its leaders buried in giant jar coffins. It is the textbook picture of a place braced for war — and one of the candidates for Yamatai itself.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Real excavation only began in 1986, after the land was slated for an industrial park, and it has been going ever since across a 117-hectare site ringed by a V-shaped outer moat about 1.6 miles (2.5 km) long. The violence was not hypothetical: skeletons came out of the jar coffins with arrowheads still lodged in the bone and heads missing entirely. The site also yielded around 33 of the same triangular-rimmed bronze mirrors that some scholars link to Himiko's hundred Wei mirrors — one more thread tying Yoshinogari into the Yamatai puzzle.

events.label: Han Bronze Mirrors
events.description: Polished bronze mirrors from Han China turned up in elite Yayoi graves across Kyushu and western Honshu — prestige objects that advertised a chief's link to the Chinese court. Local craftsmen began copying them, faithfully reproducing the Chinese cosmic designs without grasping what they meant.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The classic Han design is the 'TLV' mirror, named for the T-, L-, and V-shaped marks cast into the back, which together map a tiny model of the universe: a square earth inside a circular heaven, guarded by the four directional beasts — the green dragon of the east, white tiger of the west, red bird of the south, and entwined turtle-and-snake of the north. The marks themselves echo a Han divination board used to read the future, so the owner was meant to sit symbolically at the center of the cosmos. Centuries later these mirrors fed straight into Japanese myth: the sun goddess Amaterasu's sacred mirror became one of the three Imperial Regalia of Japan, still central to the throne today.

events.label: Gold Seal of the King of Na
events.description: In 57 CE the Han emperor Guangwu handed a gold seal to an envoy from the Kingdom of Na in Kyushu — the earliest firmly documented contact between Japan and China. Then, in 1784, a farmer fixing an irrigation ditch in northern Kyushu dug up a tiny gold seal that matched the Chinese record exactly.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The seal is astonishingly small and dense: a cube about 0.9 inches (2.3 cm) on a side weighing 108 grams, made of 95% pure gold, topped with a coiled-snake handle, its base engraved with five characters reading 'King of Na of Wa, [vassal of] Han.' The farmer, Jinbei, found it under a large stone on Shikanoshima island in Hakata Bay. It was named a National Treasure in 1931 and has anchored the Fukuoka City Museum since the museum opened in 1990. Scholars have occasionally floated forgery theories, but the seal's style fits other genuine Han seals granted to frontier vassals, and most experts treat it as the real thing.

events.label: Wa: A Hundred Kingdoms
events.description: Around 100 BCE, Chinese chroniclers gave Japan its first appearance in any written record anywhere, calling the islands 'Wa' and describing a patchwork of over a hundred small kingdoms perpetually at war. The picture matches the archaeology: hundreds of fortified Yayoi settlements competing for the best rice land.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The line comes from the 'Book of Han' (compiled in the first century CE), whose geography treatise notes that the people of Wa lived across the sea from the Lelang Commandery — a Chinese colonial outpost set up in 108 BCE around modern Pyongyang, North Korea — and that they were 'divided into more than one hundred communities' who sent tribute from time to time. So the Chinese were not sailing to Japan; they were hearing about it through their toehold in Korea. The very first written words about Japan, in other words, are secondhand notes filed by a frontier bureaucracy roughly 600 miles (970 km) away.

events.label: Queen Himiko of Yamatai
events.description: Himiko, a shaman queen of the Yamatai confederation, sent envoys to China's Wei dynasty in 238 CE. She is the first ruler of Japan recorded in writing — by the Chinese, since her own people had none — and nearly every detail about her remains contested, including where Yamatai even was.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chinese court's reply, preserved in the chronicle known as the Wei Zhi, granted her the grand title "Queen of Wa Friendly to Wei," plus a gold seal with a purple ribbon and a hundred bronze mirrors — gifts many scholars try to match to mirrors later dug from Japanese tombs. When she died, the account says, a huge mound was raised over her and a hundred attendants followed her in death; a male successor failed, civil strife broke out, and order returned only when a thirteen-year-old kinswoman named Iyo (or Toyo) was made queen in her place.

events.label: Wei Zhi Account of Wa
events.description: The Wei Zhi ("Records of Wei") is the Chinese chronicle that preserves everything we know about Himiko and third-century Japan. Its short account of the Wa people, compiled around 297 CE, is the densest single window into prehistoric Japan that survives anywhere.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It is not actually a standalone book. The Wa material is one section — fascicle 30 — of the much larger Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), written by the Chinese historian Chen Shou, who served the Western Jin dynasty that had just swallowed the Wei. In Japan the passage gets its own name, the Gishi Wajinden ("the Account of the Wa People in the Records of Wei"). Its famously slippery sailing directions are measured in li, an ancient Chinese unit of distance whose exact length in this text scholars still cannot agree on — which is a big reason nobody can pin Yamatai to a single spot on the map.

events.label: Iyo, Successor to Himiko
events.description: When Himiko died, Yamatai tried a male ruler, the country fell back into bloody chaos, and order returned only when a thirteen-year-old female relative named Iyo was made queen. The system, it turned out, needed a woman at the top.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Iyo's name also turns up spelled Toyo in older readings, and the Chinese said her installation cost roughly a thousand lives before the fighting stopped. By the time her envoys reached China in 266 CE, the Wei dynasty was gone — overthrown the year before by the Western Jin — so her tribute actually went to a brand-new Chinese emperor, Wu of Jin. After that mission the Chinese records on Japan fall completely silent for about a century and a half, leaving Iyo as the last named ruler of Wa before the long documentary blackout.

events.label: Himiko's Tomb (Hashihaka)
events.description: The Hashihaka Kofun in Nara Prefecture is the leading candidate for Himiko's grave: a keyhole-shaped mound built right around the time she died, in the region where the later imperial state would take root. If it is hers, it ties Japan's emperors directly back to the shaman-queen.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Radiocarbon dating of pottery dug from its moat puts the tomb's construction at roughly 240 to 260 CE — squarely on Himiko's death date. The mound runs about 278 meters (912 feet), with the round rear half rising some 30 meters (98 feet) high. Officially, though, it is off-limits: the Imperial Household Agency lists it not as Himiko's but as the tomb of Princess Yamatototohimomosohime, a legendary daughter of the equally legendary Emperor Korei, and bars excavation. So the Himiko theory, championed since the work of scholar Shinya Kasai, rests entirely on dating and location rather than anything found inside.

events.label: First Keyhole-Shaped Kofun
events.description: Around 250 CE, enormous keyhole-shaped burial mounds — a round mound fused to a flat-topped trapezoid, a shape you can only really see from the air — began rising in central Japan. The form is found nowhere else on Earth, and the tombs would grow to staggering size.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Japanese term is zenpo-koen-fun ("front-square, back-round mound"). The tradition climaxed two centuries later with the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, attributed to the legendary Emperor Nintoku: at roughly 486 meters (1,594 feet) long it has a larger footprint than the Great Pyramid of Giza, making it by surface area the biggest tomb on the planet. Estimates suggest it took on the order of sixteen years and a daily workforce of around 2,000 people to raise. These mounds give the whole next era — the Kofun period — its name.

events.label: Haniwa Clay Figures
events.description: Terracotta haniwa — clay figures of warriors, horses, houses, dancers, and musicians — ringed the slopes and bases of kofun mounds rather than going inside the burial chamber, giving us almost the only visual record of what Kofun-period Japan looked like.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The earliest haniwa weren't figures at all but plain clay cylinders, evolved from ceremonial jar-stands used on Yayoi-era chiefs' graves in the Kibi region (modern Okayama), and only later did potters start sculpting people, animals, and objects. The word means roughly "circle of clay," a nod to the rings they formed around a mound. A folk tradition recorded in the Nihon Shoki even claims the figures were invented as humane substitutes so that living attendants would no longer have to be buried alive with a dead ruler.

events.label: Yamato Court Consolidates Power
events.description: From the Kinai region around modern Nara and Osaka, the Yamato clan built a loose overlordship across much of Honshu and northern Kyushu — held together not by a state apparatus but by marriage alliances, ritual prestige, and a shared myth of descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: How far Yamato's reach really ran shows up on a 73.5 cm (29-inch) iron sword dug from the Inariyama mound in Saitama, far to the east near modern Tokyo: an X-ray in 1978 revealed 115 gold-inlaid characters naming a great king "Wakatakeru" — almost certainly the ruler the chronicles call Emperor Yuryaku — dated to 471 CE. A man buried 250 miles (400 km) from the capital proudly recorded serving that king, hard proof Yamato authority was felt across the islands. The same king, written as "Bu," sent envoys to China's Liu Song court in 478 begging recognition as military overlord of Wa and parts of Korea.

events.label: Cult of Amaterasu
events.description: The Yamato claim of descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu became the bedrock of imperial legitimacy, and the Ise Grand Shrine — traditionally founded in this era — was built to house her sacred mirror, one of the three imperial regalia.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By legend the shrine's site was chosen by Princess Yamatohime, who wandered the country for some twenty years carrying Amaterasu's mirror until the goddess declared from Ise, "this is a secluded and pleasant land; here I wish to dwell." The mirror, the Yata no Kagami, is still sealed inside and reportedly never seen even by the chief priest. Most strikingly, the shrine's inner sanctuary has been torn down and rebuilt from scratch on an adjacent plot every twenty years for over a millennium in a rite called Shikinen Sengu — the latest rebuild was in 2013, so the "ancient" buildings are always brand new.

events.label: Uji Clan System
events.description: Yamato Japan was run by uji — extended clans claiming descent from a common ancestor god, each tied to a particular kami and a hereditary court role. The great houses (Soga, Mononobe, Nakatomi, Otomo) held those posts and jockeyed for influence around the royal family.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Rank within this system was marked by a hereditary title called a kabane, attached to the clan name like a badge of standing at court. The rivalries turned lethal: in 587 the pro-Buddhist Soga crushed the pro-Shinto Mononobe in open battle, wiping that clan out as a political force. The Nakatomi, court ritualists who lost that round, had the last laugh — their descendant Nakatomi no Kamatari toppled the Soga in 645 and was rewarded with a new surname, Fujiwara, the family that would dominate the Japanese court for the next five centuries.

events.label: Be Occupational Groups
events.description: Below the uji aristocracy, the be system bundled commoners into hereditary occupational groups — weavers, potters, scribes, smiths, salt-makers — each attached to a clan or to the royal court. Many be began as Korean immigrants whose specialized skills made them indispensable.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The be supplied not just crafts but the court's working departments, overseen by managers called tomo-no-miyatsuko who answered to the great clans. The naming was literal: the kanuchi-be worked metal, the kinunui-be wove silk, the ama-be fished. It was hereditary but not slavery — be members were free in personal status, simply locked by birth into a trade and a patron — and the whole arrangement was swept away in the seventh-century Taika reforms that replaced clan service with a Chinese-style tax-and-province bureaucracy.

events.label: Legend of Emperor Jimmu
events.description: Later Japanese chronicles credit Emperor Jimmu with founding the imperial line in 660 BCE as a descendant of the sun goddess. The date is almost certainly invented — back-calculated to fit Chinese calendar cycles — but it served the political purpose of making imperial authority older than any foreign influence.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki his full name is Kamuyamato Iwarebiko, and the texts give him a reign of 660 to 585 BCE and a fantastical lifespan of 127 years. Modern scholars treat him as legend — there were no states of any scale in Japan in 660 BCE — yet the myth still anchors the modern calendar: February 11 is National Foundation Day, marking his supposed accession, and a wartime imperial era counted years from 660 BCE, making 1940 the "2,600th year" of the dynasty.

events.label: Introduction of Chinese Writing
events.description: According to the much later Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, a scholar named Wani arrived from the Korean kingdom of Baekje carrying the Confucian 'Analects' and the 'Thousand Character Classic,' bringing Chinese writing to the Yamato court. The legend is shaky, but the underlying truth — that literacy reached Japan via Korea — holds up.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: There is a glaring crack in the story: the 'Thousand Character Classic,' the primer Wani supposedly carried, wasn't even written until the early sixth century CE, well over a hundred years after his traditional arrival date. So the texts can't be literally true as told. Edo-period scholars noticed the snag centuries ago — Arai Hakuseki (1657–1725) guessed the chroniclers had simply confused which beginner's book Wani brought. Wani is also claimed as a founding ancestor by certain old Japanese clans, which is one reason the tale got polished and preserved. The real arrival of sustained literacy in Japan came later still, in the fifth and sixth centuries.

events.label: Daisen Kofun Built
events.description: Near modern Sakai City south of Osaka, the keyhole-shaped Daisen Kofun rose to roughly 1,600 feet (486 meters) long across some 80 acres — the largest tomb in the world by surface area, built without writing, coinage, or a Chinese-style bureaucracy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In 1872 a storm collapsed part of the slope and briefly exposed a stone sarcophagus along with armor, a gilded helmet, and glass bowls before the breach was resealed — about the only glimpse anyone has ever gotten inside, since the Imperial Household Agency still forbids excavation. Including its triple moat and outer banks the whole footprint stretches roughly 2,700 feet (840 meters) end to end, and its slopes once bristled with an estimated 29,000 terracotta haniwa figures. In 2019 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site at the heart of the Mozu-Furuichi cluster of mounded tombs.

events.label: Mounted Warriors and Horse Armor
events.description: Around 400 CE horses, riveted iron-plate armor, and mounted combat appear suddenly in Japan — all imported from Korea, and all over the haniwa and grave goods of the fifth century. The old 'horse-rider theory' said conquering Korean cavalry founded Yamato; today scholars favor cultural borrowing over invasion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before this point there's essentially no trace of horses in Japan at all; afterward the islands fill up with horse bones, bridle bits, stirrups, and equine haniwa. The conquest version was floated in 1948 by archaeologist Egami Namio, who imagined a horse-riding people sweeping down from the Asian mainland to take over — a striking idea that has since lost favor for lack of any sign of a violent takeover. The likelier story is that Yamato elites, plugged into Korea through Baekje and Gaya, simply bought, copied, and absorbed the era's cutting-edge military kit.

events.label: Baekje-Yamato Alliance
events.description: Baekje, the southwestern of Korea's Three Kingdoms, was Yamato Japan's closest ally and main pipeline for continental technology. Its princes were sometimes raised at the Yamato court as honored hostages, and its envoys ferried craftsmen, scholars, and eventually Buddhism across the strait.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tradition credits a Baekje scholar named Wani with bringing the first Chinese books to Japan — copies of the Analects of Confucius and a primer called the Thousand Character Classic — though that last text was written too late for the story to be literally true. The alliance's most famous relic is the Seven-Branched Sword, a 74.9 cm (29.5-inch) iron blade with six branch-like prongs and a gold-inlaid inscription, sent from a Baekje king and still kept (unseen by the public) at the Isonokami Shrine near Nara. Baekje's King Geunchogo, who cemented ties with Yamato, ruled in the mid-to-late fourth century.

events.label: Gaya Iron Trade
events.description: The Gaya confederacy, a cluster of small states on the southern tip of Korea, produced some of East Asia's finest iron and shipped it to Japan in bulk. Gaya was a cultural and economic bridge between Yamato and the Korean kingdoms, though the extent of Japanese involvement in its politics is hotly contested.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gaya grew straight out of the earlier Byeonhan polities of the Nakdong River basin, who were already iron specialists; its merchants traded standardized iron ingots that doubled as a kind of currency across the region. The heartland state, Geumgwan Gaya, sat at modern Gimhae. Squeezed between bigger neighbors, the confederacy was slowly devoured by Silla — Geumgwan Gaya fell in 532 and the last holdout, Daegaya, was conquered in 562, ending Gaya for good and cutting off one of Japan's key iron lifelines.

events.label: Mimana Controversy
events.description: The Nihon Shoki, compiled in 720 CE, claims Yamato Japan ran a colonial outpost called Mimana in southern Korea from the late fourth century. Most modern Japanese and Korean scholars judge the claim badly inflated — likely a later projection of imperial ambition back onto the Kofun era.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The fiercest battleground for this dispute is the Gwanggaeto Stele, a towering stone monument in Manchuria raised in 414 to a Korean Goguryeo king, which records that from the "Sinmyo year" of 391 the Wa (the Japanese) crossed the sea and warred in Korea. Japanese historians long read it as proof of Mimana; Korean scholars read the same worn characters very differently, and some even accused early-twentieth-century investigators of tampering with the inscription. What's not disputed is that Yamato and southern Korea were knit together by trade, migration, marriage, and military alliance — a relationship too tangled for either side's nationalist storytelling to capture.

events.label: Korean Artisans and Technology Transfer
events.description: Across the late Kofun period, immigrants from the Korean kingdoms of Baekje and Gaya — the 'toraijin' — kept arriving with the skills Yamato wanted: iron smelting, silk weaving, sueki stoneware, horse breeding, and continental-style building. So many settled and intermarried that a striking share of the aristocracy later claimed continental roots.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'roughly a third' figure has a hard source: the Shinsen Shōjiroku, a register of noble families compiled in 815 CE, lists 326 of 1,182 clans in the capital region as being of foreign (mostly Korean) descent — about 28 percent. Two of the giants were the Hata, fabulously wealthy from sericulture and engineering and now usually traced to Silla, and the Yamatonoaya, who supplied scribes and skilled craftsmen. These weren't a despised underclass: many toraijin lineages sat among the court elite, and their literacy in Chinese would become indispensable to the writing-based state that followed.

events.label: Sueki Stoneware
events.description: Sueki — a hard, gray, wheel-thrown stoneware fired in oxygen-starved tunnel kilns at over 1,800°F (1,100°C) — arrived from southern Korea around 450 CE and became the prestige ceramic of choice. It was tougher and more durable than anything Japan had made before, and it needed imported Korean know-how to produce.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The technique came in on a specific piece of kit: the 'anagama,' a sloped tunnel kiln dug into a hillside that Korean potters brought over and that let temperatures climb far past the open bonfires of earlier ware. The biggest early production zone, the Suemura kiln complex, sprawled across the hills of what is now southern Sakai and neighboring cities in Osaka Prefecture — sitting right beside the Mozu tomb cluster, so the same landscape was turning out both elite pottery and emperor-scale graves. The craft is widely traced to the Kaya (Gaya) region of southern Korea, the same area that had long been Yamato's iron supplier.

events.label: Domestic Iron Production
events.description: By around 500 CE Japan started smelting its own iron instead of buying it all from Korea — clay bloomery furnaces in western Honshu burned local iron sand (satetsu) raked from rivers and beaches. This was the seed of the 'tatara' tradition that would one day forge the samurai's swords.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Japan went the iron-sand route because the islands are short on the rich iron-ore deposits that fed continental smelters, so smiths leaned on the iron-rich black sands of the Chugoku mountains instead. A classic tatara run is a brutal marathon: a clay furrow furnace fed alternating layers of iron sand and charcoal, burning nonstop for about three days and nights — roughly 70 hours — consuming around 12 tons each of sand and charcoal to yield about 1.5 tons of steel bloom (kera) plus pig iron. The resulting prized steel, 'tamahagane,' is still made this way for traditional swordsmiths today.

events.label: Late Kofun Tomb Decline
events.description: Around 500 CE the great keyhole-tomb tradition went into decline — mounds shrank, fewer got built, and the old clan competition to out-monument the neighbors faded. It is the archaeological fingerprint of a Yamato state stable enough that the elite no longer had to advertise their rank in dirt.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Just how much labor the peak tombs swallowed is staggering: the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka (attributed to the legendary Emperor Nintoku), runs about 1,594 feet (486 meters) long and is often estimated to have taken roughly 16 years and more than 2,000 workers a day to raise, with three moats and once as many as 29,000 clay 'haniwa' figures ringing its tiers. By surface area and volume it outsizes both the Great Pyramid of Giza and the First Qin Emperor's mausoleum. The Mozu cluster it anchors became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

events.label: Emperor Keitai
events.description: Keitai (reigned roughly 507–531 CE) is the earliest Japanese emperor most historians treat as genuinely real rather than legendary. Court factions pulled him in from outside the Yamato heartland after the old royal line died out heirless — and the patched-on family tree linking him back to earlier emperors looks like later spin to keep the 'unbroken line' story alive.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He came from Echizen, in the Koshi region of northern Honshu, well off the Kinai stage where Yamato kings usually emerged, which is why scholars often read his reign as the start of a 'new dynasty.' The Nihon Shoki makes him a fifth-generation descendant of Emperor Ojin through a prince named Wakanuke no Futamata — a chain too convenient and too distant for many historians to swallow. Notably, he didn't even rule from the traditional Yamato basin at first, only shifting his capital into what became Yamato Province around 526, a hint at how shaky an outsider's grip on the heartland could be.

events.label: Iwai Rebellion
events.description: In 527 CE Iwai, the powerful local lord of Tsukushi in northern Kyushu, rose against the Yamato court — reportedly cutting a deal with Korea's Silla kingdom to choke off Yamato's military traffic to the peninsula. It took heavy fighting to put him down, exposing how loose Yamato's hold on Kyushu really was.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Keitai handed the campaign to the warrior clan chief Mononobe no Arakabi, and by 528 Iwai had been beaten and killed; the court then locked the region down, a process that fed into the later founding of the Dazaifu government outpost that ran Kyushu for centuries. Iwai's likely resting place still stands: the Iwatoyama Kofun in Yame, Fukuoka, the largest tomb in northern Kyushu, whose early-6th-century date (pinned by its sueki pottery) lines up neatly with the chronicles. Its grounds are studded with carved stone figures of people, horses, and shields — a regional burial style quite unlike the Kinai keyhole tombs.

events.label: Soga Clan Rises
events.description: The Soga clan climbed to the top of the Yamato court in the early 500s with a fresh playbook: instead of grabbing the old military and priestly offices, they cornered foreign trade and the labor of Korean immigrants, then married their daughters into the royal family. That positioned them perfectly to back the new religion about to arrive from Baekje.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The man who drove the rise was Soga no Iname (about 506–570), who held the top minister's rank of Ō-omi and was the first court grandee to openly push for adopting Buddhism. When Baekje's Buddhist gifts came, he reportedly took the images home to Mukuhara (in today's Asuka, Nara) and turned his own house into Japan's first Buddhist temple. The feud he started ran for generations: his son Soga no Umako crushed the rival Mononobe in 587, and the whole Soga line was finally toppled by the Nakatomi heir Kamatari in the 645 coup known as the Isshi Incident.

events.label: Buddhism Arrives at the Yamato Court
events.description: In 538 CE King Seong of Baekje shipped a gilt-bronze Buddha and a set of sutras to the Yamato court, recommending Japan take up the faith — the diplomatic delivery that conventionally ends Japanese prehistory. The Soga embraced it; the Mononobe and Nakatomi fought it, kicking off a religious-political war that ran for decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The famous 538-versus-552 date split is real: the official court chronicle Nihon Shoki puts the gift in 552 under Emperor Kinmei, while the older Gangōji temple history says 538 — and most modern scholars trust the temple's 538. Seong (reigned 523–554) wasn't being purely pious; he was a Buddhist king who'd just moved his capital to Sabi and badly needed Yamato as a military ally against rival Korean states, so the statue doubled as a sweetener for an alliance, and his envoys reportedly even included pagoda-builders and roof-tile makers. According to one tradition, the Guze Kannon statue still kept at Hōryū-ji temple was carved as a likeness of Seong himself.
